episodes.title: Jews Are Blind
episodes.summary: The haftara opens with God as Creator, then calls Israel a covenant people meant to be a light to the nations, yet “blind” and “deaf.” With the Malbim, Rabbi Dweck reads the blindness as praise: only those who have tried to see know how much they cannot see, as Newton and the Rambam said of themselves.

moments.note: The opening nod to Bereshit: “I am God who created the heavens and laid out the earth.”
“I have made a covenant with My people, set them as a light to the nations.”
“To open blind eyes”: sight as understanding, and the morning blessing pokeach ivrim.
A shirah chadashah, a new song, sung by those who know their own blindness.
“I have long held My peace”: God will no longer stay hidden from those who search.
“I will lead the blind by a way they did not know”: the Rambam and Newton, brought into the light.
The Malbim: only someone who has sight to lose can be called blind.
“Who is blind but My servant?” The blind are the ones always striving to see.
The Ashkenazi reading goes on to “I love you”: this is not a rebuke.

episodes.title: Beautiful People
episodes.summary: God promises Israel, abandoned and widowed, that His covenant is like the oath of the waters of Noah: the mountains may crumble, His kindness will not. Rabbi Dweck turns to suffering and what comes after it, from Frankl to the Holocaust survivors who rebuilt, to Kübler-Ross: “Beautiful people don’t just happen.”

moments.note: Israel as a widow: the shame and vulnerability of a woman left alone.
“Fear not, for you shall not be ashamed”: the source of Lecha Dodi’s lo tevoshi.
God speaks as Israel’s husband, in the feminine.
“Yes, I have scorned you and left you”: the spousal frame of the prophets.
“For a small moment I forsook you”: it was only for a short time.
“Like the waters of Noah”: the haftara’s link to the parasha, and to God’s oath.
“The mountains may depart”: one of the most loving verses in Tanakh.
Why the Jewish people came through: the mountains crumble, God does not move.
